sections.title: Definitions of key terms

summary.text: Defines key terms used in the guidelines, including age groups for adults, adolescents, children and infants and WHO's definition of key populations. It also explains concepts such as substantial risk of HIV and notes that risk-informed PrEP can be cost-effective but that cost should not be the only consideration.

sections.extract: Age groups In these guidelines the following definitions for adults, adolescents, children and infants are used in recommendations for specific age groups. It is acknowledged that countries may have other definitions under national laws. • An adult is a person older than 19 years of age. • An adolescent is a person 10–19 years of age inclusive. • A child is a person from one year of age to younger than 10 years of

sections.title: Purpose

summary.text: Explains that reaching the 2025 target of 95% access to HIV prevention requires more prevention choices, recalling WHO's 2015 oral PrEP and 2021 dapivirine ring recommendations and slow uptake. It presents the guideline's purpose of recommending long-acting cabotegravir using a public health approach and highlighting implementation considerations.

sections.extract: Achieving the Global AIDS target for 2025 of ensuring that 95% of people at risk of HIV acquisition have access to HIV prevention options requires a focus on expanding effective HIV prevention choices. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a key component of combination HIV prevention. sections.title: Guideline development methodology

summary.text: Describes how the cabotegravir recommendation was developed between January and May 2022 by WHO with a Guideline Development Group and External Review Group, based on a PICO question and systematic reviews. It states that the group judged the evidence of moderate certainty and unanimously made a conditional recommendation to offer long-acting cabotegravir as an additional prevention choice.

sections.extract: In response to the availability of new evidence on the efficacy of CAB-LA for the prevention of HIV acquisition, external experts and stakeholders proposed to make this recommendation as an addition to the HIV prevention recommendations in the 2021 Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring (3). As a result, from January to May 2022, the WHO Department of Global

sections.title: Implications for implementation

summary.text: States that long-acting cabotegravir should be offered alongside oral PrEP and the dapivirine ring within comprehensive prevention, noting that provision has so far been mostly limited to trials. It lists implementation considerations and research needs, such as HIV testing strategies, service delivery models, drug resistance, safety in pregnancy and cost-effectiveness, with full community participation.

sections.extract: CAB-LA should be delivered as an additional choice alongside other PrEP options, including oral PrEP and the DVR, as part of a comprehensive HIV prevention approach. To date, provision of CAB-LA has largely been limited to trial settings, certain geographies and specific populations. This guideline outlines operational research needed to address research and implementation gaps, and to inform decisions on how to

sections.title: Background

summary.text: Describes the global HIV situation, with about 37.7 million people living with HIV and 1.5 million new infections in 2020, a decline well short of global targets, and high shares among key populations and young women in sub-Saharan Africa. It recalls the 2021 Political Declaration targets and WHO's existing PrEP recommendations. It explains the case for additional PrEP options and notes that risk-informed PrEP can be cost-effective while having value beyond cost.

sections.extract: HIV remains a major public health issue, with approximately 37.7 [30.2–45.1] million people living with HIV and 1.5 [1.0–2.0] million new infections in 2020. Despite global commitments to reduce new infections by 75% between 2010 and 2020, to fewer than 500 000, new HIV infections declined only by 31% over that decade (4). sections.title: Objective and intended audience

summary.text: Sets out the objective of providing an evidence-informed recommendation on cabotegravir as PrEP and names the intended audiences, from national programme managers and clinicians in low- and middle-income countries to people at risk, community organizations and donors.

sections.extract: This guideline is intended to provide an evidence-informed recommendation for CAB-LA as PrEP for HIV prevention to support countries in achieving national targets of reducing new HIV infections. The primary audience for this guideline is national and subnational programme managers and policy-makers responsible for the national health sector response to HIV, particularly in LMICs, and clinicians and other health care

sections.title: Guiding principles

summary.text: Lists the guiding principles for implementing the cabotegravir guideline, including a public health and universal health coverage approach, equity and human rights, voluntary and stigma-free services. It also stresses adapting to local context and full participation of affected communities.

sections.extract: The following principles have informed the development of this guideline and should guide the implementation of the recommendations: • This guideline needs to be implemented within a public health and universal health coverage framework. In addition to strengthening HIV prevention services, the guideline should be implemented with a view to strengthening broader health systems, especially primary and community-based

sections.title: Methods for guideline development

summary.text: Explains that the guideline followed WHO Guidelines Review Committee procedures and the GRADE approach, with declarations of interest from all external contributors. It lists the web annexes of evidence prepared and presented at meetings facilitated by an independent methodologist.

sections.extract: This guideline was developed in accordance with procedures established by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee (16). The recommendation in this guideline is based on the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach to reviewing evidence and formulating recommendations (17). sections.title: Summary of review findings

summary.text: Summarizes the systematic review of four randomized trials of long-acting cabotegravir, the efficacy studies HPTN 083 and 084 and the safety studies ECLAIR and HPTN 077, enrolling about 8,120 people. It reports a 79% reduction in HIV risk compared with oral TDF/FTC, largely explained by poor adherence to daily pills, and describes breakthrough and other infections. It reviews modelling for Atlanta, Montreal, South Africa and sub-Saharan Africa on the infections that expanded or switched PrEP could avert. It then covers safety, finding no significant difference in adverse events, limited pregnancy data without congenital abnormalities, and no reported differences in STIs.

sections.extract: Evidence on the safety, efficacy and effectiveness of CAB-LA was collected in a systematic review of research on CAB-LA (Web Annex B) and from additional unpublished preliminary results from modelling presented to the GDG (18, 19). sections.title: Cost–effectiveness

summary.text: Reviews seven costing studies, mostly from South Africa, and new models showing mixed results on whether long-acting cabotegravir is cost-effective. It finds it could be cost-effective in some settings or groups, for example in South Africa if focused on periods of substantial risk and priced within twice the cost of oral PrEP, but not compared with generic oral PrEP in high-income settings.

sections.extract: Evidence on cost–effectiveness of CAB-LA was derived from a systematic review (Web Annex B) and additional modelling evidence presented to the GDG (Web Annexes D and E) (19, 23). The review identified seven studies that assessed the cost or cost–effectiveness of CAB-LA or long-acting PrEP more generally. sections.title: Values and preferences

summary.text: Summarizes evidence on acceptability and preferences from a review of 99 studies, key population networks and a provider survey, showing general interest in injectable PrEP with variation between groups. It notes providers' concerns about cost, workload, testing, drug resistance and stopping the drug, and the potential to overcome adherence problems with daily pills.

sections.extract: Evidence on acceptability, values and preferences for CAB-LA was derived from a systematic review of publications on injectable PrEP (Web Annex C), results of qualitative research from four global key population networks and a study on the perspectives of PrEP providers (Web Annex F). A systematic review identified 99 articles meeting inclusion criteria for the values and preferences analysis (Web Annex C). Most

sections.title: Feasibility

summary.text: Notes that long-acting cabotegravir has been used only in trials, among adult cisgender women and among cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men, with no evidence yet for people under 18. It points to experience with oral PrEP and injectable contraceptives and flags the need to explore feasibility for sex workers, people who inject drugs, prisoners and transgender men.

sections.extract: Both HPTN 083 and HPTN 084 implemented CAB-LA for PrEP in a range of countries for adult cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men and for cisgender women at risk of HIV. No studies have demonstrated the feasibility of this intervention in individuals under the age of 18 years, although studies are ongoing. sections.title: Equity

summary.text: States the guideline group's view that offering cabotegravir could improve equity by reaching more people who prefer injections, but that unequal access between and within countries could widen health inequalities.

sections.extract: HIV prevention among PrEP users will contribute to equitable health outcomes by sustaining their health and the health of their sexual partners. Access to PrEP also provides opportunities for access to sexual and reproductive health services addressing multiple health needs. sections.title: Rationale for recommendation

summary.text: States the conditional recommendation that people at substantial risk of HIV may be offered long-acting injectable cabotegravir as an extra prevention option, based on moderate-certainty evidence. It explains the group's reasoning about benefits, uncertainties and costs as a barrier, and describes people for whom it may suit, such as those valuing discretion or struggling with oral pills.

sections.extract: Recommendation Long-acting injectable cabotegravir may be offered as an additional prevention choice for people at substantial risk of HIV infection, as part of combination prevention approaches (conditional recommendation; moderate certainty of evidence). The GDG agreed that CAB-LA for PrEP could have substantial benefits, a judgment based on evidence of moderate certainty, as well as on acceptability to

sections.title: HIV testing and other testing requirements

summary.text: Sets out HIV testing requirements for cabotegravir, with testing before starting, before each injection and ideally after stopping, using national serology algorithms and further testing for reactive or inconclusive results. It warns that missed or delayed diagnosis during use or in the drug's long pharmacokinetic tail could lead to integrase-inhibitor resistance, and weighs the uncertain benefits, costs and practical limits of adding nucleic acid testing. It also covers hepatitis B and C considerations and states that kidney function monitoring is not required.

sections.extract: As with oral PrEP and the DVR, HIV testing is required before offering CAB-LA and should also be done before each injection while using CAB-LA and, ideally, regularly after CAB-LA discontinuation. HIV testing can be conducted according to the WHO testing strategy for HIV diagnosis in people >18 months of age, using the national testing algorithm composed of quality-assured serology assays (that is, rapid diagnostic

sections.title: Service delivery

summary.text: Discusses service delivery for long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA) as HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis, noting that experience so far comes mainly from two trials while oral PrEP has been offered in many settings. It suggests that such settings, and PrEP services offering a wider package of care, could support CAB-LA, with meaningful involvement of key populations and young people.

sections.extract: CAB-LA provision to date has been limited to the two RCTs, with some further experience emerging from the unblinded open-label extensions of the RCTs. Services for oral PrEP, however, have been implemented in a range of settings in many countries. These include primary health care clinics, sexual and reproductive health services, ante- and post-natal care services and in community settings through, for example, key

sections.title: Comprehensive services

summary.text: Recommends offering PrEP, including CAB-LA, alongside other prevention and health services such as condoms, PEP, STI and hepatitis care, mental health support, gender-affirming care and harm reduction.

sections.extract: PrEP, including CAB-LA, should be provided in combination with other effective and well- established prevention approaches and health services. Depending on the local context and the needs and preferences of the populations that could benefit from PrEP, this may include the provision of condoms, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV, testing and treatment of STIs and viral hepatitis, sexual and reproductive health

sections.title: Offering a choice of PrEP options

summary.text: Advises that a range of PrEP options, including oral PrEP, the dapivirine ring and CAB-LA, be available, with counselling so people can make an informed choice.

sections.extract: People who could benefit from PrEP have diverse HIV prevention needs and preferences, and these may change over time. A range of PrEP options should be available to provide choice to people who could benefit from PrEP, including TDF-based oral PrEP, the DVR and CAB-LA. sections.title: Involving communities

summary.text: Lists good participatory practices for involving communities in PrEP and CAB-LA programmes, such as funding community-led organizations, building their capacity and expanding community-based services. It also calls for coercion-free choice and for decriminalizing consensual sex, gender expression, sex work and drug use.

sections.extract: Meeting the needs of populations at substantial risk of HIV infection and providing PrEP services, including CAB-LA, requires the full participation of communities in developing and implementing programmes. The following are good participatory practices that apply to services for all priority and key populations: • Recognize the leadership and resilience of priority and key populations in addressing the HIV epidemic

sections.title: Creating awareness and demand

summary.text: Recommends awareness programmes for communities and providers before and during the introduction of CAB-LA, engaging key population networks to build acceptance and demand.

sections.extract: As CAB-LA is a new PrEP product, many communities and providers have limited or no awareness of it. Countries wanting to introduce CAB-LA as an additional HIV prevention option should conduct an awareness programme for communities and providers before and during introduction as a first step towards creating demand and enabling people to make informed choices. Engagement with networks of individuals who could benefit

sections.title: Adherence support and discontinuation

summary.text: Explains that CAB-LA and other PrEP products are meant for times when HIV risk is substantial, and that trial infections occurred mainly with delayed injections or after stopping. It describes the declining protection during the drug's pharmacokinetic tail, the associated resistance risk and counselling on injection-site reactions and other side-effects.

sections.extract: PrEP products, including CAB-LA, should be used during periods of substantial HIV risk and may be stopped if an individual is no longer at risk or decides to use an alternative PrEP product or HIV prevention strategy. The two RCTs on CAB-LA found CAB-LA highly effective at preventing HIV when CAB-LA was administered on time, although a few cases of HIV acquisition, despite on-time injections, were observed. sections.title: Training and support for providers

summary.text: Describes the training providers will need to deliver CAB-LA, building on oral PrEP experience, including discussing prevention preferences, administering injections and offering respectful, non-judgemental services. It anticipates that training needs will become clearer as implementation expands.

sections.extract: As CAB-LA is a new PrEP product, few PrEP providers will have experience delivering CAB- LA. However, there is extensive experience with delivering oral PrEP. National programmes should provide training and support to a range of providers in services that may be able to offer CAB-LA to clients. Training for providers will include capacity building on discussing HIV prevention needs and preferences with clients;

sections.title: Research gaps and needs

summary.text: Calls for operational research, designed with affected communities, to guide CAB-LA implementation and scale-up.

sections.extract: Operational research is needed to inform decisions on the implementation and scale-up of CAB-LA. It is important to partner with communities of populations affected by HIV to identify priorities and to inform the design and implementation of research and the monitoring of outcomes.

sections.title: Providing CAB-LA for key populations

summary.text: Identifies research gaps for CAB-LA among key populations, noting that trials included few transgender men or non-binary people and no people who use drugs. It highlights needs such as data on gender-affirming hormones, alternative injection sites and monitoring of access barriers.

sections.extract: HPTN 083 and HPTN 084 provided PrEP to cisgender men who have sex with men, transgender women (approximately 2.5% of participants) and cisgender women. However, the studies included few transgender men and did not specify including non-binary individuals. Further research is required to evaluate CAB-LA service delivery for trans and gender-diverse people and their specific needs and preferences. The trials on CAB-LA

sections.title: CAB-LA for adolescents under age 18

summary.text: Notes that people under 18 were excluded from the main CAB-LA trials and that adolescent studies are planned, calling for operational research on acceptability and support for young people.

sections.extract: Individuals under age 18 were not included in ECLAIR, HPTN 077, HPTN 083 or HPTN 084, although sizable numbers of study participants were under the age of 30. Small numbers of adolescents have been included in ongoing sub-studies for HPTN 083 (38) and 084 (39). Additional studies including adolescent and young people are planned. These will contribute evidence on CAB-LA safety and acceptability among adolescent men

sections.title: Safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding

summary.text: Discusses limited data on CAB-LA safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding, noting trial contraception requirements and the open-label extension allowing continued use under monitoring. It calls for further research and links to contraceptive and antenatal services.

sections.extract: In some settings pregnancy and the postpartum period are characterized by increased risk of acquiring HIV. HIV acquired during pregnancy or breastfeeding is associated with a risk of HIV transmission to the infant. It is important that women of reproductive potential do not face barriers to uptake of effective HIV prevention options such as CAB-LA. sections.title: Optimal HIV testing strategies and drug resistance

summary.text: Identifies uncertainty about optimal HIV testing strategies during CAB-LA use as a critical research gap, including risks of delayed diagnosis and drug resistance. It calls for studies on testing frequency, alternative assays and cross-resistance between cabotegravir and dolutegravir.

sections.extract: As noted in section 4.1, the optimal HIV testing strategies, testing frequency and general approaches throughout CAB-LA implementation remain uncertain and constitute a critical research gap. Some key issues include (1) risk of delayed HIV diagnosis and treatment, (2) implications for HIV drug resistance, (3) optimal strategies for establishing HIV infection post- CAB-LA initiation and (4) feasibility and

sections.title: Service delivery models

summary.text: Notes that oral PrEP is delivered through varied services with task sharing, whereas CAB-LA has so far been used only in trials. It calls for implementation research on offering CAB-LA alongside other options, including different injection schedules, self-injection and community delivery.

sections.extract: Oral PrEP has been delivered through a range of services, including services for STIs and sexual and reproductive health, antenatal and postnatal care and primary health care, and in a range of settings, including clinics, pharmacies and the community. Task sharing among a range of health care providers, such as nurses and trained lay providers, is playing an increasingly prominent role in the delivery of PrEP. This

sections.title: Population-level impact and costs and cost–effectiveness

summary.text: Reports preliminary modelling suggesting that expanding total PrEP use has the largest effect on HIV incidence and that CAB-LA could be cost-effective in sub-Saharan Africa, while calling for more realistic models and cost studies.

sections.extract: effectiveness Preliminary results of mathematical modelling suggest that increasing the total number of PrEP users, whether of oral PrEP or CAB-LA, has the strongest impact on decreasing HIV incidence (Web Annexes D and E) (23). CAB-LA use itself has the potential to increase the number of HIV infections averted. Models for sub-Saharan Africa also suggest that CAB-LA could be cost-effective even if priced higher

sections.title: Updating and dissemination

summary.text: Describes how the CAB-LA guideline will be published online with its web annexes, incorporated into WHO's consolidated HIV guidelines and disseminated with regional and country offices, with uptake tracked through a country policy database.

sections.extract: This guideline is being launched as a web-based product for dissemination and will include all evidence as presented to the GDG (Web Annexes A to F). The guideline will also be incorporated into the periodic updates of the WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV (3). sections.title: Annex 1. Process for developing the guidelines

summary.text: An annex describing how the CAB-LA guideline was developed under WHO guideline standards and Guideline Review Committee oversight, coordinated by the Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis and STI Programmes. It outlines the systematic review of safety and efficacy, supplementary evidence on values, costs and feasibility, and how the Guideline Development Group reached its recommendation. The annex closes with contact details and the ISBN.
